lessons.title: Forces that change the Earth’s surface

videos.title: Internal and external forces, plate tectonics (parent to choose)

warmup.back: Landforms are natural features on the Earth’s surface, such as mountains, valleys, plains and plateaus.

cards.title: Landforms
cards.body: The lithosphere is not even and the same everywhere. It is made up of many different kinds of landforms. "Landforms are natural features on the Earth’s surface, such as mountains, valleys, plains and plateaus."

cards.title: Two kinds of forces
cards.body: The surface of the Earth, and the landforms on it, constantly undergo changes due to the action of various forces. These forces are of two types—internal forces and external forces.

cards.title: Internal (tectonic) forces
cards.body: "Internal forces, or tectonic forces, are forces acting from within the Earth that lead to sudden changes on the face of the Earth." The stiff and brittle lithosphere is broken up into several pieces called tectonic plates. They float over the viscous molten rock, called magma.

cards.title: Plate tectonics
cards.body: Heat from the core of the Earth heats the magma in the mantle. The heated magma rises, spreads, cools and then sinks again. These rising and sinking streams of magma push against the tectonic plates, causing them to move. This movement of the plates is termed plate tectonics.
cards.reveal: Plates converge (move towards each other), diverge (move away from each other), or slide by each other in a transverse movement.

cards.title: Slow… and sudden
cards.body: The plates move very slowly (just a few centimetres in a year), so mountains and valleys can take millions of years to form. But sometimes sudden and strong movements bring about massive changes: earthquakes, volcanoes and landslides.
cards.didYouKnow: Internal forces are also known as endogenetic or endogenic forces.

cards.title: External (gradational) forces
cards.body: "External forces, or gradational forces, are forces acting from above on the surface of the Earth." They lead to slow and steady changes, by wearing away and rebuilding the Earth’s surface. They are also called exogenic or denudational forces, and include all the agents of gradation like wind, water and glaciers.
cards.example: Weathering (breaking down rocks into smaller bits), eroding (transporting the weathered material) and depositing it at other places. Rain, wind and rivers erode the mountains and deposit the material further down to form plains.

practice.explanation: Internal forces, or tectonic forces, act from within the Earth (p.44).

practice.prompt: The movement of the tectonic plates is termed ____.
practice.explanation: This movement of the plates is termed plate tectonics (p.45).
hints: Two words: the second one rhymes with "electronics".

practice.prompt: When two plates move towards each other, they
options: slide by in a transverse movement
practice.explanation: Towards each other = converge; away from each other = diverge (p.45).

practice.prompt: Put the work of the agents of gradation in order.
sequence: Weathering: breaking rocks into smaller bits
Depositing the material at other places
practice.explanation: Rocks are first broken down, then carried away, then laid down somewhere else (p.45).
hints: You have to break the rock before you can carry the bits away.

lessons.notebook: Make a two-column table in your notebook: Internal forces | External forces. For each, write its other names, how it acts (sudden, or slow and steady) and examples (pp.44–45).

check.prompt: External forces lead to sudden changes on the Earth’s surface.
check.explanation: External forces lead to slow and steady changes. Internal forces cause sudden changes (pp.44–45).

check.prompt: Which of these is an agent of gradation?
check.explanation: The agents of gradation are like wind, water and glaciers (p.45).

check.prompt: The stiff and brittle lithosphere is broken up into several pieces called ____.
check.explanation: "…broken up into several pieces called tectonic plates" (p.44).

check.prompt: About how fast do the tectonic plates move?
options: A few centimetres in a year
A few metres in a day
A few kilometres in a year
check.answer: A few centimetres in a year
check.explanation: The plates move very slowly, just a few centimetres in a year (p.45).

keyRules: Landforms are natural features on the Earth’s surface, such as mountains, valleys, plains and plateaus.
Internal forces, or tectonic forces, are forces acting from within the Earth that lead to sudden changes on the face of the Earth.
The movement of the plates is termed plate tectonics.
External forces, or gradational forces, are forces acting from above on the surface of the Earth.

lessons.title: Mountains: fold and block

videos.title: Fold mountains and block mountains (parent to choose)

cards.title: Three major landforms
cards.body: Geographers classify major landforms on the basis of their elevation and slope. On this basis, there are three major types of landforms—mountains, plateaus and plains.

cards.title: What is a mountain?
cards.body: "A mountain is a natural elevation of the Earth’s surface rising high above its surroundings." Mountains have narrow summits (peaks), steep slopes and broad bases. They are found both on land and on the ocean floor. A chain of mountains is called a mountain range.
cards.reveal: The higher reaches of the mountains can be very cold, because temperature falls with altitude.

cards.title: Hills and valleys
cards.body: Hills are highlands that are not as high as mountains, and have gentler slopes. The area of lowland found between hills or mountains is called a valley. Many valleys have rivers flowing through them.
cards.example: The Zanskar Mountain Range, with the rivers Zanskar and Indus flowing in their valleys.

cards.title: Fold mountains
cards.body: "Fold mountains are formed by the upliftment and folding of landmasses due to lateral compression caused by tectonic or internal forces." Where two plates converge, the crust gets compressed and crumpled or folded, and massive layers get uplifted.
cards.didYouKnow: Lateral compression means to be squeezed from both sides. Try it: push the ends of a stack of floor mats towards each other and watch folds form in the centre!

cards.title: Young and old fold mountains
cards.body: The Himalayas and the Alps were formed in the recent geological past, so they are young fold mountains. They have rugged relief, and high, sharp peaks. The Aravalli Range in Rajasthan is one of the oldest fold mountain ranges in the world; it has been lowered greatly by continuous erosion.
cards.example: The Urals in Russia and the Appalachians in North America are also very old fold mountains.

cards.title: Block mountains
cards.body: When two plates diverge or get pulled apart, fractures called faults appear. When two faults form alongside each other, the land between them either subsides (falls) or gets uplifted (rises). The uplifted part is called a horst or block mountain; the subsided part is called a graben or rift valley.
cards.example: The Narmada River flows through a rift valley. The Rhine Valley in Europe is a rift valley, and the Black Forest and Vosges Mountains beside it are block mountains.

practice.prompt: A chain of mountains is called a
practice.explanation: A chain of mountains is called a mountain range (p.45).
They were formed in the recent geological past, so they are young fold mountains (p.46).

practice.prompt: The uplifted part of the land between two faults is called a ____ or block mountain.
practice.explanation: Uplifted part = horst (block mountain); subsided part = graben (rift valley) (p.47).

practice.prompt: Put the steps in order: how fold mountains form.
sequence: Two plates move towards each other
The place where they meet gets compressed
The crust gets crumpled or folded
Massive layers get uplifted: fold mountains
hints: It starts with the plates moving.

lessons.notebook: Draw two simple diagrams in your notebook: (1) fold mountains, with arrows pushing from both sides; (2) block mountains, with two faults, a horst and a graben. Label each (pp.46–47).

check.explanation: Hills are highlands that are not as high as mountains, with gentler slopes (p.45).

check.prompt: Which of these is one of the oldest fold mountain ranges in the world?
check.explanation: The Aravalli Range in Rajasthan is one of the oldest fold mountain ranges (p.46).

check.prompt: The Narmada River flows through a ____ valley.
check.explanation: The Narmada River flows through a rift valley (p.47).

check.prompt: Fold mountains form where two plates
check.explanation: Fold mountains: plates converge. Block mountains: plates diverge (pp.46–47).

keyRules: A mountain is a natural elevation of the Earth’s surface rising high above its surroundings.
Fold mountains are formed by the upliftment and folding of landmasses due to lateral compression caused by tectonic or internal forces.
When two plates on the Earth’s crust diverge or get pulled apart, fractures appear on the Earth’s surface. These fractures are called faults.
The uplifted part of the land is called a horst or block mountain, and the subsided part is called a graben or rift valley.

lessons.title: Volcanic mountains and plateaus

videos.title: Volcanic mountains and types of plateaus (parent to choose)

cards.title: Volcanic mountains
cards.body: Sometimes, conical or dome-shaped structures are formed as a result of magma escaping to the surface of the Earth through an opening called a vent. These are called volcanic mountains, or volcanoes. "Magma that reaches the surface of the Earth is called lava."

cards.title: How a volcano builds up
cards.body: The lava, ash and rocks that erupt from the volcanoes settle in layers on the surface of the Earth. Over thousands of years, these layers build up and volcanic mountains are formed.
cards.example: The book’s diagram labels: magma under pressure, vent, crater, lava, and gases, ashes & cinders.

cards.title: Gentle or steep?
cards.body: If the magma is thin and flows easily, gently sloping mountains are formed, such as Mauna Loa in Hawaii. If the lava is thick and viscous, the mountains are cone-shaped with steeply sloping sides.
cards.example: Mt Vesuvius in Italy, Mt Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, Africa and Mt Fuji in Japan.

cards.title: Plateaus
cards.body: "A plateau is a broad, flat, elevated area of land that rises sharply above the surrounding area." It is also called a tableland. A plateau may have one gently sloping side and one steep side. The steep side of a plateau is called an escarpment.

cards.title: Famous plateaus
cards.body: The largest and highest plateau in the world is the Tibetan Plateau (4,000–6,000 m above mean sea level). The Pamir Plateau and the Tibetan Plateau are both called the ‘roof of the world’.
cards.didYouKnow: The Deccan Plateau in India is one of the oldest plateaus of the world, and most of the African continent is made of plateaus.

cards.title: Three types of plateaus
cards.body: Intermontane plateaus are surrounded completely or partially by mountains (the plateau of Tibet). Continental plateaus are vast areas of tableland that rise abruptly from the coast or surrounding plains (the plateaus of Africa). Lava plateaus form when lava flows out of fissures and spreads thickly over extensive areas (the Deccan Plateau).

practice.prompt: Magma escapes to the surface of the Earth through an opening called a ____.
hints: It is also a word for an air hole.

practice.prompt: Thick, viscous lava forms mountains that are
practice.explanation: Thin, runny magma → gentle slopes. Thick, viscous lava → steep cones (p.47).
hints: Thick lava doesn’t flow far before it stops.

practice.prompt: The steep side of a plateau is called
practice.explanation: The steep side of a plateau is called an escarpment (p.47).
hints: It is in the Words to Remember on p.49.

practice.prompt: Match each type of plateau with the book’s example.
practice.explanation: p.48 gives one example for each type.
hints: Tibet is surrounded by mountains: "inter-montane" means between mountains.

lessons.notebook: Draw the structure of a volcano in your notebook and label: magma under pressure, vent, crater, lava, and gases, ashes & cinders (p.47). Then write the three types of plateaus with one example each (p.48).

check.prompt: A plateau is also called a tableland.
check.explanation: It is also called a tableland (p.47).
Thin magma that flows easily formed gently sloping Mauna Loa (p.47).

check.prompt: Which is the largest and highest plateau in the world?
check.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau, 4,000–6,000 m above mean sea level (p.47).

check.prompt: The Deccan Plateau is a ____ plateau.
check.explanation: "The Deccan Plateau is a lava plateau" (p.48).

keyRules: Magma that reaches the surface of the Earth is called lava.
A plateau is a broad, flat, elevated area of land that rises sharply above the surrounding area. It is also called a tableland.
The steep side of a plateau is called an escarpment.
Plateaus are of three types: intermontane, continental and lava plateaus.

lessons.title: Plains, and landforms and people

videos.title: Plains and how landforms affect people (parent to choose)

cards.title: Plains
cards.body: "A broad area of relatively flat land is called a plain." Generally plains are low-lying: their average height is just around 200 m above mean sea level.

cards.title: Alluvial tracts
cards.body: Most plains are levelled alluvial tracts, formed by the deposits brought down by rivers and their tributaries. Rivers bring down eroded material, called alluvium, from the mountains: sand, silt, clay, and animal and plant matter. These rich nutrients make highly fertile alluvial tracts.

cards.title: Famous plains
cards.body: The Nile Basin in Egypt, the Hwang Ho Basin in China and the Indo-Gangetic Basin in India are some examples of plains.
cards.example: The book also shows the Russian Plain.

cards.title: Landforms shape our lives
cards.body: Landforms influence the climate of a place, the type of houses people build, their occupations, the clothes they wear, the availability of water, and the crops grown.

cards.title: Mountains and plateaus help us
cards.body: Mountains: most of the rivers in the world originate in the mountains. Mountains bring rain, and act as barriers against both hot and cold winds. Plateaus: rich deposits of minerals such as iron ore, gold and bauxite, and fossil rocks such as coal. Their waterfalls are important sources of hydro-electric power.

cards.title: Plains and people
cards.body: Plains, being fertile and largely flat, are the main crop growing regions of the world. It is easier to build roads and railway networks there. So plains are the most densely populated regions on Earth.
cards.reveal: But people have made homes in every kind of terrain, by modifying the land to suit their needs and adapting their own lifestyle.

practice.prompt: Eroded material brought down from the mountains by rivers is called ____.
practice.explanation: alluvium: eroded material brought down from the mountains by rivers (p.49).

practice.prompt: The average height of plains is just around
practice.explanation: Plains are low-lying, around 200 m above mean sea level (p.48).

practice.prompt: Waterfalls on plateaus are important sources of
practice.explanation: Waterfalls found on plateaus are important sources of hydro-electric power (p.48).

practice.prompt: Match each landform with how it helps people.
practice.explanation: p.48: Importance of mountains, plateaus and plains.

lessons.notebook: Make the book’s 3-tab foldable (p.49): Forces that change the Earth’s surface · Different types of landforms · Landforms and people. On a map, mark the Deccan Plateau, the Aravalli range, the Alps, the Urals, Mt Fuji, Mt Kilimanjaro, the plateau of Tibet and the Nile Basin (Ex. VI, p.51).

check.prompt: Plains are the most densely populated regions on Earth.
check.explanation: Plains are, therefore, the most densely populated regions on Earth (p.49).

check.prompt: The Indo-Gangetic Basin is an example of a
check.explanation: The Indo-Gangetic Basin in India is one of the book’s examples of plains (p.48).

check.prompt: Mountains act as barriers against both hot and cold ____.
check.explanation: "…acting as barriers against both hot and cold winds" (p.48).

check.prompt: Plateaus have rich deposits of minerals such as
check.explanation: Iron ore, gold and bauxite are plateau minerals. Sand, silt and clay are in alluvium (p.48).

keyRules: A broad area of relatively flat land is called a plain.
Alluvial tracts are formed by the deposits brought down by rivers and their tributaries.
Landforms influence the climate of a place, the type of houses people build, their occupations, the clothes they wear, the availability of water, and the crops grown.
Plains are the most densely populated regions on Earth.

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following is a major agent of gradation or denudation?
questionBank.explanation: The agents of gradation include wind, water and glaciers. Earthquakes and volcanoes come from internal forces (p.45).

questionBank.prompt: Why do we not feel the movement of the tectonic plates?
questionBank.modelAnswer: Because the plates move very slowly, just a few centimetres in a year.
questionBank.explanation: p.45: the plates move very slowly (just a few centimetres in a year).

questionBank.prompt: Most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries. Why do you think this is so?
questionBank.modelAnswer: The plates move towards each other, away from each other, or slide by each other. Where the plates meet, sudden and strong movements can take place, and these cause earthquakes.
questionBank.explanation: Use p.45: how plates move, and that sudden strong movements cause earthquakes.

questionBank.prompt: Explain how external forces cause changes on the surface of the Earth.
questionBank.modelAnswer: External (gradational) forces act from above on the surface of the Earth. They cause slow and steady changes by wearing away and rebuilding the surface. Agents of gradation like wind, water and glaciers do this by weathering (breaking down rocks into smaller bits), eroding (transporting the weathered material) and depositing it at other places. For example, rain, wind and rivers erode mountains and deposit the material further down to form plains.
questionBank.explanation: p.45 has every part of this answer.

questionBank.prompt: Weathering means ____ rocks into smaller bits.
questionBank.explanation: Weathering (breaking down rocks into smaller bits) (p.45).

questionBank.prompt: Internal forces are also known as endogenic forces.
questionBank.explanation: Internal forces are also known as endogenetic or endogenic forces (p.45).

questionBank.prompt: The Alps and the Urals are ____ mountains.
questionBank.explanation: The Alps are young fold mountains and the Urals are old fold mountains (p.46).

questionBank.prompt: Fractures in the Earth’s crust are called ____.
questionBank.explanation: These fractures are called faults (p.46).

questionBank.prompt: The land that subsides between two faults is called a ____.
questionBank.explanation: The subsided part is called a graben or rift valley (p.47).

questionBank.prompt: The book shows a picture of mountains. We can say with certainty that they are mountains because: (i) they have sharp peaks (ii) they have steep sides (iii) they rise high above the surroundings (iv) they are covered in snow.
questionBank.explanation: A mountain rises high above its surroundings, with narrow summits (peaks) and steep slopes (p.45). Snow is not part of what makes a mountain.

questionBank.prompt: The Satpura Range in central India was formed as a result of land getting uplifted along fault lines. It is a:
questionBank.explanation: Land uplifted between fault lines is a horst or block mountain (p.47).

questionBank.prompt: Name the three main types of landforms of the world.
questionBank.explanation: There are three major types of landforms—mountains, plateaus and plains (p.45).

questionBank.prompt: Explain the process of plate tectonics. How does it lead to the formation of fold mountains?
questionBank.modelAnswer: Heat from the core of the Earth heats the magma in the mantle. The heated magma rises, spreads, cools and sinks again. These rising and sinking streams push against the tectonic plates and make them move; this is plate tectonics. When two plates move towards each other (converge), the place where they meet gets compressed (lateral compression). The crust there gets crumpled or folded, and massive layers get uplifted, forming fold mountains, like the Himalayas and the Alps.
questionBank.explanation: Plate tectonics is on pp.44–45; fold mountains on p.46.

questionBank.prompt: How are block mountains formed? How are they different from fold mountains?
questionBank.modelAnswer: When two plates diverge (get pulled apart), fractures called faults appear. When two faults form alongside each other, the land between them is displaced vertically: the uplifted part is a horst or block mountain, and the part that subsides is a graben or rift valley. Fold mountains are different: they form when plates converge, and the crust is compressed, folded and uplifted.
questionBank.explanation: Block mountains: pp.46–47. Fold mountains: p.46.

questionBank.prompt: Magma that reaches the surface of the Earth is called ____.
questionBank.explanation: Magma that reaches the surface of the Earth is called lava (p.47).

questionBank.prompt: Mt Kilimanjaro is a ____ mountain.
questionBank.explanation: Mt Kilimanjaro is one of the book’s steep, cone-shaped volcanic mountains (p.47).

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following statements about plateaus is correct?
options: Plateaus are broad, flat lands rising sharply above the surrounding areas.
Only Asia and Africa have plateaus.
Plateaus are the most densely populated regions of the world.
questionBank.answer: Plateaus are broad, flat lands rising sharply above the surrounding areas.
questionBank.explanation: This matches the definition on p.47. A plateau may have one gently sloping side, and plains (not plateaus) are the most densely populated.

questionBank.prompt: Describe the formation of volcanic mountains with the help of a diagram.
questionBank.modelAnswer: Magma under pressure escapes to the surface of the Earth through an opening called a vent. Magma that reaches the surface is called lava. The lava, ash and rocks that erupt settle in layers on the surface. Over thousands of years these layers build up and form a conical or dome-shaped volcanic mountain. (Draw the volcano: magma under pressure, vent, crater, lava, and gases, ashes & cinders.)
questionBank.explanation: p.47 has the steps and the diagram. Draw it in your notebook too.

questionBank.prompt: How are mountains different from plateaus?
questionBank.modelAnswer: A mountain rises high above its surroundings and has a narrow summit (peak), steep slopes and a broad base. A plateau is a broad, flat, elevated area of land (a tableland) that rises sharply above the surrounding area; it may have one gently sloping side and one steep side (an escarpment).
questionBank.explanation: Mountains: p.45. Plateaus: p.47.

questionBank.prompt: Distinguish between intermontane plateaus and continental plateaus.
questionBank.modelAnswer: Intermontane plateaus are surrounded completely or partially by mountains, for example, the plateau of Tibet. Continental plateaus are vast areas of tableland that rise abruptly from the coast or surrounding plains, for example, the plateaus of Africa.
questionBank.explanation: Both are on p.48.

questionBank.prompt: Which two plateaus are both called the ‘roof of the world’?
options: The Pamir Plateau and the Tibetan Plateau
The Deccan Plateau and the Tibetan Plateau
The Pamir Plateau and the Waterberg Plateau
questionBank.answer: The Pamir Plateau and the Tibetan Plateau
questionBank.explanation: p.47: the Pamir Plateau to the north of India and the Tibetan Plateau.

questionBank.prompt: Assertion (A): Plains are the most densely populated parts of the world. Reason (R): People find it convenient to live in the plains.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not a complete explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questionBank.answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
questionBank.explanation: Plains give better conditions for living and it is easier to build roads and railways, so they are the most densely populated (pp.48–49).

questionBank.prompt: What are plains? How are they formed? Why do people prefer to live on plains?
questionBank.modelAnswer: A broad area of relatively flat land is called a plain; plains are low-lying, about 200 m above mean sea level. Most plains are alluvial tracts: rivers bring down alluvium (sand, silt, clay, and animal and plant matter) from the mountains and deposit it, forming highly fertile land. People prefer plains because they are fertile and largely flat, they are the main crop growing regions, and it is easier to build roads and railways there, so living conditions are better.
questionBank.explanation: pp.48–49 have every part of this answer.

questionBank.prompt: Plains are formed in different ways. Most of them are levelled ____ tracts.
questionBank.explanation: "Most of them are levelled alluvial tracts" (p.48).

questionBank.prompt: The Nile Basin is in
questionBank.explanation: The Nile Basin in Egypt (p.48).

questionBank.prompt: People live only in the plains.
questionBank.explanation: People have made their homes in every kind of terrain, by modifying the land and adapting their lifestyle (p.49).
